B1.title: New LED Technology Breaks Record
B1.body: Scientists from several universities have made a big discovery. They found a way to make blue light-emitting diodes (LEDs) more efficient. LEDs are used in many devices, like phones and TVs. The researchers are from Peking University, Eindhoven University of Technology, and other schools. They worked together to solve a problem with blue LEDs. These LEDs are made with special materials called perovskites. Perovskites are great for LEDs because they shine very brightly. However, they have a problem. When they are made, they can be either very bright or very small, but not both. The researchers found a way to make them both bright and small. They used a special method to control how the perovskites grow. This method is called polymerization-driven nanocrystal confinement. It helps the perovskites grow in a way that makes them very efficient. The researchers were able to make LEDs that are 21.8% efficient. This is a very high rate. The discovery is important because it could lead to better LEDs. These LEDs could be used in many devices, making them brighter and more efficient. The researchers are happy with their discovery and think it could lead to big changes. They worked hard to solve the problem and are proud of their result. Their work could help make many devices better.

B2.title: Breakthrough in Blue Perovskite LEDs
B2.body: A team of researchers from several top universities, including Peking University and the Eindhoven University of Technology, has made a significant breakthrough in the development of blue perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs). The researchers have found a way to overcome a major challenge in creating high-efficiency PeLEDs, which has held back their development for some time. Metal halide perovskites are highly attractive for LED applications due to their excellent luminescence properties. However, achieving both high crystallinity and small crystal size has been a fundamental contradiction during the formation of nanocrystals. Small nanocrystals are essential for efficient radiative recombination, yet they are typically prone to structural disorder and defect formation. On the other hand, larger crystals exhibit improved crystallinity but reduced emission efficiency. To address this issue, the researchers developed an in situ polymerization approach. This approach involves the use of polymerizable ligands that coordinate with perovskite precursor species during film formation. These ligands then form a polymer network that imposes nanoscale spatial confinement on the growing nanocrystals, limiting crystal growth while maintaining sufficient structural flexibility for lattice reorganization. This breakthrough has enabled the creation of high-efficiency devices with an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 21.8%. The implications of this discovery are significant, as it could lead to the development of more efficient and cost-effective LEDs. The researchers' approach has the potential to resolve the long-standing trade-off in blue PeLEDs, paving the way for further innovation in the field.

C1.title: Breakthrough in Perovskite LEDs
C1.body: A significant breakthrough has been achieved by researchers from Peking University, Eindhoven University of Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Institute of Technology, and University of Science and Technology of China. They have successfully developed an effective strategy to resolve a long-standing trade-off in blue perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs). This innovative approach enables the creation of high-efficiency devices through polymerization-driven nanocrystal confinement. Metal halide perovskites are highly attractive for LED applications due to their excellent luminescence properties. However, device performance has been constrained by a fundamental contradiction during in situ nanocrystal formation. The contradiction arises from the need to achieve both high crystallinity and small crystal size. Small nanocrystals are essential for efficient radiative recombination, yet they are typically prone to structural disorder and defect formation. In contrast, larger crystals exhibit improved crystallinity but reduced emission efficiency. To address this challenge, the researchers developed an in situ polymerization approach. In this approach, polymerizable ligands coordinate with perovskite precursor species during film formation. These ligands subsequently form a polymer network that imposes nanoscale spatial confinement on the growing nanocrystals. This confinement limits crystal growth while maintaining sufficient structural flexibility for lattice reorganization, thereby enabling the creation of high-efficiency PeLEDs with an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 21.8%. The significance of this breakthrough lies in its potential to revolutionize the field of LED technology, enabling the development of more efficient and sustainable devices. The researchers' innovative approach has successfully resolved the long-standing trade-off, paving the way for the widespread adoption of perovskite LEDs in various applications. Furthermore, this achievement demonstrates the power of interdisciplinary collaboration and the importance of continued research in the field of materials science.
